# Bibliography Management in LaTeX

This guide outlines the different methods for managing references, ranging from manual entry to modern automated systems.

- OverLeaf links:
  - [bibtex](https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Bibliography_management_with_bibtex)
  - [natbib](https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Bibliography_management_with_natbib)
  - [biblatex](https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Bibliography_management_with_biblatex)

## Comparison of Reference Systems

| System | Automation Level | Style Control | Primary Benefit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Zero Reference Manager | Manual  | Hard-coded  | No external files or packages required. |
| BibTeX | Automatic  | .bst files  | Separates data (.bib) from document structure. |
| natbib | Automatic  | .bst files  | Adds author-year citation support to BibTeX. |
| biblatex | Automatic  | LaTeX commands  | High flexibility, modern, and faster performance. |

## Manual Method: Zero Reference Manager

This approach is entirely manual, requiring you to order, style, and write every entry yourself.

* *Environment*: Create a `thebibliography` environment at the end of your document.
* *Entries*: Use `\bibitem{key}` to define individual references within that environment.
* *In-text Citation*: Use the `\cite{key}` command to reference the entry in your text.

```latex
\begin{thebibliography}{9}
\bibitem{texbook}
Donald E. Knuth (1986) \emph{The \TeX{} Book}, Addison-Wesley Professional.
\end{thebibliography}
```

## Automated Method: BibTeX

BibTeX is a program that automatically generates the bibliography for you.

### 1. The .bib File
You store your bibliography entries in a plain text `.bib` file. These entries follow a specific format (e.g., `@book`, `@article`) and include fields for author, title, year, and other metadata.

```latex
@book{latexcompanion,
    author    = "Michel Goossens and Frank Mittelbach and Alexander Samarin",
    title     = "The \LaTeX\ Companion",
    year      = "1993",
    publisher = "Addison-Wesley",
    address   = "Reading, Massachusetts"
}
```

### The Workflow

The automated bibliography process involves a sequence of file generations:

* *The Wish List*: Your LaTeX engine generates an auxiliary file (`.aux`) that contains every citation key used in the document.
* *The Processing*: The `bibtex` program reads this `.aux` file, retrieves the matching entries from your bibliography database (`.bib`), and generates a bibliography file (`.bbl`) containing the formatted entries.
* *The Inclusion*: The engine then pastes the content of that `.bbl` file directly where the `\bibliography{<bib_file>}` command is located in your document.
* *Automation*: These multiple processing runs are handled automatically by Overleaf (which uses `latexmk` in the background) and by Quarto or RMarkdown during the rendering process.
* *Styling*: You can determine how entries are formatted (e.g., `plain`, `alpha`, or `abbrv`) by specifying a style with the `\bibliographystyle{<style>}` command.

---

### Enhanced Citation: natbib

While `bibtex` can be used alone, the `natbib` package is commonly loaded to provide expanded citation features:

* *Citation Style*: Standard BibTeX is often limited to numerical citations like `[1]`. `natbib` enables author-year citations, such as `(Einstein, 1905)`.
* *Implementation*: To use these features, include the package in your preamble.

```latex
\usepackage{natbib}
```

* *Commands*: Once loaded, you can use `\cite{}` for standard references, `\citet{}` for textual citations, or `\citep{}` for parenthetical citations.
* *Final List*: Place the `\bibliography{<bib_file>}` command in your document body where you want the reference list to appear.
* *Limitations*: Customizing styles in `natbib` is notoriously difficult because it relies on editing complex `.bst` files, such as `plain.bst`.

---

### The Modern Standard: biblatex

`biblatex` is a modern alternative that offers significantly more flexibility and control over your bibliography:

* *Ease of Customization*: Formatting is performed directly within LaTeX using `biblatex` commands, which are much easier to modify than external `.bst` files.
* *Speed*: It is generally faster than the traditional `bibtex` program.
* *Implementation*: Add the package and the database resource to your preamble.


```latex
\usepackage[style=authoryear]{biblatex}
\addbibresource{<bib_file>.bib}
```

* *Commands*: Cite your sources using `\cite{}`, `\textcite{}` (textual), or `\parencite{}` (parenthetical).
* *Printing*: Use the `\printbibliography` command to render the reference list in your document.

# `R` in `LaTeX`

We can both display `R` code as text and run `R` code to include results in our document.

## Displaying `R` code

To include R code as text without executing it (e.g., in an appendix), the **`minted`** package is the gold standard. It provides superior syntax highlighting compared to the basic `listings` package and handles long lines of code gracefully.

* **Pygments Highlighting**: `minted` uses Python-based highlighting, which correctly identifies R functions and variables.
* **Customization**: By setting global options, you can ensure consistent font sizes and line numbering across your entire document.
* **Technical Note**: Ensure your Overleaf compiler is set to **pdfLaTeX**, **XeLaTeX**, or **LuaLaTeX**. Overleaf handles the `-shell-escape` requirement automatically for the `minted` package.

### 1. Preamble Configuration

Add the following to your preamble to set the global style for your R code:

```latex
\usepackage{minted}

\setminted{
    fontsize=\small,
    breaklines=true,
    linenos,
    frame=lines
}
```

The above settings define the visual style of your code blocks as follows:

* **`fontsize=\small`**: Scales the code text down slightly to fit more content on each line and improve readability.
* **`breaklines=true`**: Automatically wraps long lines of code so they stay within the page margins instead of overflowing.
* **`linenos`**: Enables line numbering on the left side of the block, making it easy to reference specific lines in your writing.
* **`frame=lines`**: Places horizontal rules above and below the code snippet to clearly separate it from the surrounding text.

### 2. Including your Code

In your document, you can include an external R script file or write the code directly in the LaTeX editor.

**To include an external file:**

```latex
\inputminted{r}{your_script.R}
```

**To write code inline:**

```latex
\begin{minted}{r}
# This is an R comment
summary(cars)
plot(cars)
\end{minted}
```

## Running `R` code

For documents requiring dynamic data or analysis, Overleaf allows you to execute R code directly within your project. This is achieved using the `knitr` engine, which processes code chunks and inserts the results into your final PDF.

### Core Requirements

* **File Extension**: You must rename your primary file from `main.tex` to `main.Rtex` for Overleaf to recognize and execute the R code.
* **Engine Support**: This environment is specifically designed for `knitr`; other methods like `\input{*.Rtex}` are generally not supported.
* **Documentation**: For official guidance, refer to the [Overleaf knitr documentation](https://docs.overleaf.com/integrations-and-add-ons/r-code-knitr#Introduction).

```latex
<<chunk-name, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE>>=
# R code goes here
# echo=TRUE displays the code in the PDF
# eval=FALSE prevents the code from running
@
```

### `R` code written in the `LaTeX` file

```latex
<<>>=
# R code goes here
@
```

- Chunks can have names, e.g.

```latex
<<chunk-name>>=
# R code here
@
```
- Standard `knitr` chunk options apply, such as `echo=TRUE` to show the code, `eval=FALSE` to not run the code, etc. For example:

```latex
<<chunk-name, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE>>=
# R code here
@
```

Refer to results with `\Sexpr{}`, e.g. `The result is \Sexpr{2 + 2}.` or `The result is \Sexpr{mean(x)}.` where `x` has been defined in a previous chunk.

### Inline R Code

You can embed R results directly into your text without creating a full block. This is useful for citing specific statistics or variables.

* **Syntax**: Use the `\Sexpr{}` command.
* **Example**: "The mean value is `\Sexpr{mean(data)}`."

### Managing External R Scripts

If you prefer to keep your R code in a separate `.R` file, you can import it into your `main.Rtex` document using the `read_chunk` function.

**Tag the Script**: In your `.R` file, identify chunks using a specific comment header: `## ---- chunk-label`. For example:

```r
## ---- chunk-name-1
# R code here

## ---- chunk-name-2
# R code here
```

**Load the File**: Read the script into your LaTeX document using a code chunk:

```latex
<<>>=
read_chunk("my_script.R")
@
```

The first chunk is automatically run.

**Reference the Label**: To display or run a specific part of that script later, use a LaTeX chunk with the matching label name. For example:

```latex
<<chunk-name-2, echo=TRUE>>=
@
```

As you can see, a `knitr` chunk option was used. Any `knitr` chunk option is valid here.

### Visualizing Data

When you generate plots, `knitr` handles the figure environment and labeling automatically.

* **Labeling**: The name you give the chunk becomes the LaTeX label, automatically prefixed with `fig:`.
* **Referencing**: You can reference a plot named `myplot` using `\ref{fig:myplot}`.
* **Captions**: Use the `fig.cap` option within the chunk header to define the figure's title.

```latex
<<histogram-plot, fig.pos="t", fig.height=4, fig.width=4, fig.cap="Standard Normal Distribution">>=
set.seed(2)
hist(rnorm(100), main="Sample Histogram", xlab="Value")
@

The figure \ref{fig:histogram-plot} shows a histogram of 100 random normal values.
```
### The R Environment on Overleaf

The R environment on Overleaf differs significantly from a local setup.

* **R Version**: Overleaf currently uses R version 3.6.3. This version was released in 2020 and precedes major updates found in R 4.0 and later.
* **Compatibility**: Features like the native pipe operator (`|>`) are unavailable, as they require R 4.1 or higher.
* **Package Limitations**: You are limited to the packages pre-installed in the Overleaf `R` environment. You can get a full list by adding the following to your `main.Rtex` file:

```latex
<<>>=
pkgVec <- installed.packages()[, "Package"] 
pkgVecNull <- setNames(pkgVec, NULL) 
sort(pkgVecNull)
@
```

# Overcoming Overleaf limitations

## Collaboration

On the free plan, you can only have two editors per project.
If you have more than two people, you have several options:

- Paying \$ 10  per month or \$ 98 per year for the Student plan.
- Use a view link for all group members, and remove people not currently writing anything.

## Compile timeouts

On the free plan, you have a shorter compile time limit and slower servers, and some documents may not compile in time.
Again, you have several options:

- Pay for the Student plan, which has a longer compile time limit and faster servers.
- Optimise your document to reduce compile time, such as by:
  - Using PDF images instead of PNGs or SVGs.
  - Compiling parts of the document separately and reading them with `\includepdf[pages=-]{file.pdf}`.
    - This will require fiddling with page numbers to make them follow on correctly.
  - Following other advice from Overleaf: https://docs.overleaf.com/troubleshooting-and-support/fixing-and-preventing-compile-timeouts#steps-to-resolve-compile-timeouts

# Quarto/RMarkdown versus Overleaf

- You control the `R` environment fully, so can install packages, use any version of `R`, etc.
- No compile time limit. 
- Will need to set up `LaTeX` locally.
- Easiest to do this with the `tinytex` package in `R`, which provides a lightweight distribution of `LaTeX` that is easy to install and manage:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
```

Beyond basic alignment with amsmath, there are several "pro-tier" behaviors and alternative environments you'll likely run into when your math gets more complex.

1. The "Star" Versions (Unnumbered Equations)
By default, environments like equation and align automatically number your math on the right side of the page.

How to hide numbers: Append an asterisk (*) to the environment name, like \begin{align*} ... \end{align*}.

The amsmath benefit: While standard LaTeX has a displaymath environment, using equation* is generally preferred because it handles spacing more consistently.

2. The cases Environment
If you need to define a function that changes based on a condition (like an absolute value or a piecewise function), cases is the easiest tool.

3. Matrices and Grouping
The amsmath package provides specialized environments for matrices that handle the brackets for you:

matrix: Plain numbers.

pmatrix: Parentheses (…).

bmatrix: Square brackets […].

vmatrix: Determinant bars ∣…∣.

4. Text inside Math
If you type "if" or "where" inside a math environment, LaTeX treats it as a string of variables and removes all spacing (looking like if). Use the \text{...} command to insert normal text with proper spacing inside your equations.

Custom Gem
Gemini said
Yes, the cases environment is a core feature of the amsmath package. While amsmath is the "must-have" foundation for almost any technical document, it is usually part of a small "starter pack" of math packages you'll want to load by default.

1. Using the cases Environment
The cases environment is used for piecewise functions. It automatically adds a large left brace and handles the internal alignment.

Syntax Example:

Code snippet
\[
f(x) = 
\begin{cases} 
  \frac{1}{x} & \text{if } x \neq 0 \\
  0           & \text{if } x = 0 
\end{cases}
\]
The & symbol: Used to align the conditions (like the "if" statements).

The \\ command: Used to start a new line within the brace.

The \text{} command: Essential for writing the "if" part so it doesn't look like italicized variables.

2. Is amsmath the only package you need?
While amsmath is the most important, most users load a "Big Three" set of packages to cover all bases:

amsmath: For the logic, environments (like align, cases), and basic symbols.

amssymb: Provides a massive library of mathematical symbols (like R for real numbers or ℏ).

amsfonts: Provides specialized fonts, such as "blackboard bold" used in set theory.

The Modern Pro-Tip: Many power users now load mathtools instead of amsmath. It automatically loads amsmath but adds fixes for spacing and extra commands like \xRightarrow or better vertical alignment for matrices.

/QA [The cases Environment and Math Packages]
Source Text: The cases environment is part of the amsmath package and is used for piecewise functions. It utilizes the & symbol for alignment and \\ for line breaks. For a complete math setup, users often load amsmath, amssymb, and amsfonts. The mathtools package is a common alternative that includes amsmath while providing additional formatting fixes.
